---
title: "Engineering log"
---

Design decisions, refactors, numerical stability issues, data layout and
performance choices. It supplements the git history with the reasoning.
Entries are dated H2 sections; existing entries are never edited.

## 2026-11-05: Step 0, project scaffolding

**Double precision.** `jax_enable_x64` is set in `jaxdft/_config.py`, the
first import in `jaxdft/__init__.py`. Any entry point that imports anything
from the package therefore enables x64 before any array exists. The test suite
checks this in a fresh subprocess as well as in-process, because
`tests/conftest.py` imports `jaxdft` for every test and would otherwise hide a
broken import order.

`jaxdft.precision.assert_double_precision` walks a pytree and rejects any
inexact leaf that is not float64 or complex128. Integer and boolean leaves
(Miller indices, masks) are ignored. Physics tests should call it on their
outputs. This is how "a test must fail if any physical array is float32" is
enforced in practice.

**Test configuration.**

- `--import-mode=importlib`, so the three test directories can contain
  files with the same name without `__init__.py` packages.
- `filterwarnings = error`: a warning from JAX (e.g. an implicit dtype
  truncation) fails the test rather than scrolling past.
- `--strict-markers`, with one marker, `slow`, defined up front.
- Hypothesis runs with `deadline=None`, because the first call of a jitted
  function includes tracing and compilation, so per-example timing is
  meaningless. Two profiles: `default` (50 examples, for laptops) and `ci`
  (200), selected with `HYPOTHESIS_PROFILE`.

**Dependencies.** `pytest` and `hypothesis` are in the `dev` group, `altair`
and `jupyter` in `docs`. Both are uv default groups, since the definition of
done needs both, so a plain `uv sync` installs everything.

**Docs execution.** `execute.freeze` is explicitly `false`. Documents compute
their numbers from `jaxdft` at render time, and freezing would let a document
go stale against the code without failing.

Quarto must find the project's virtual environment. It does when the venv is
active (it then picks `.venv/bin/python3` from `PATH`). From a plain shell it
falls back to the system Python and fails. I tried a `docs/_environment` file
setting `QUARTO_PYTHON`. Quarto resolves that relative path against the
directory it is invoked from, not the project, so it broke depending on where
the command was run, and I removed it. `uv run quarto render docs/` works from
any shell and is the robust form of the definition-of-done command.

**Removed.** The `jaxdft` console-script entry point and its `main()`
placeholder from the `uv init` template. A command-line interface will be
added when there is something to run.

**Deferred.**

- The shared plot-style module arrives with the first plot (Milestone 1a
  validation). It will live outside the physics so that `altair` stays a docs
  dependency.
- A `units` module with tested conversions arrives with the first
  boundary conversion. Milestone 1a works entirely in atomic units and in
  units of $\tfrac12(2\pi/a)^2$.

## 2026-11-05: Milestone 1a design decisions from theory review

The [theory post](../theory/01a_empty_lattice.qmd) was reviewed before any
implementation. Every quantitative claim was re-derived independently, and no
physics errors were found. The review changed four engineering decisions.
I reproduced its measurements with a throwaway NumPy enumeration before
accepting them.

**Per-k padded Miller-index lists, not a shared candidate set.** `vmap` needs
a common shape, not a common set of G vectors. The first draft proposed one
set containing every $\mathcal{B}_\mathbf{k}$ (radius $G_\text{max} + |\mathrm{W}|$)
plus a per-k mask. For fcc with $a = 10.26$ Bohr over the six high-symmetry
points, that set was 1.73× the largest per-k basis at 5 Ha and 1.17× at 80 Ha.
Dense `eigh` costs the cube of that: 5.1× and 1.6×. The per-k sizes
themselves differ by about 2%. The batch layout is therefore
`(n_k, N_pad, 3)` integer Miller indices plus an `(n_k, N_pad)` boolean mask.
`N_pad` is a Python int fixed on the host before tracing. These numbers are a
one-off snapshot for the decision record; the validation document computes
them from the library.

**Padding is exactly decoupled, and the sentinel is modest.** Padded components
must have zero rows and columns, not just a large diagonal. Otherwise
$\tilde V(\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{G}')$ in 1b, evaluated at a padding entry's
arbitrary Miller index, would leak into the physical block. The sentinel
diagonal is a small multiple of $E_\text{cut}$. The reviewer measured that LAPACK's
physical eigenvalues are insensitive to the sentinel (1.9e-13 Ha for sentinels
from 4e1 to 1e12). A huge sentinel would still spread the spectrum over many
orders of magnitude, which slows down the iterative solvers planned later.
The test is solver-independent: the same k-point with two values of `N_pad`
must give the same bands.

**Provable enumeration bound.** The integer search box is
$|m_i| \le \lceil (G_\text{max}+|\mathbf{k}|)|\mathbf{a}_i|/2\pi \rceil$, from
$\mathbf{G}\cdot\mathbf{a}_i = 2\pi m_i$ and Cauchy–Schwarz. A guessed cube is
unsafe in skewed cells.

**Cutoff ties.** Test cutoffs are placed strictly between shells, with a
relative margin of at least 1e-8. The reviewer suggested instead making the
reference enumeration use the code's own arithmetic, so ties round the same
way. I did not adopt that, because it makes the reference less independent of
the code it checks.

**Basis-size bound.** The reviewer flagged that a test asserting monotone
convergence of $N_\text{PW}$ to its asymptote would be flaky, and proposed a
bound $C\,E_\text{cut}^{-1/2}$ with $C$ measured once. I used a rigorous bound
instead, from tiling with Brillouin zones of circumradius $r_\text{BZ}$, which
needs no fitted constant. A first version used the reciprocal parallelepiped's
diameter (2.03 Bohr⁻¹ at $a = 10.26$). It held, but was nearly vacuous: the
upper bound was 4.4 at 5 Ha. The Wigner–Seitz circumradius $|\mathrm{W}|$
(0.68 Bohr⁻¹) is three times tighter. It is still loose and catches only
gross errors; the exact count is tested by enumeration.

**References.** Cutoff conventions as documented for DFTK (`Ecut`), ABINIT
(`ecut`) and Quantum ESPRESSO (`ecutwfc`, `ecutrho`). No source code was
consulted.

## 2026-11-05: Milestone 1a public API, agreed before implementation

The acceptance tests fix the public API, so it was settled in a question round
with the project lead before any code was written. Each decision below names
the option that was chosen.

**Layout.** Subpackages by role in the calculation, not a flat set of modules.
The main names are re-exported from `jaxdft`.

```
jaxdft/
  structure/    lattice.py (Lattice)   kpoints.py (special_points_fcc, kpath, KPath)
  basis/        planewave.py (PlaneWaveBasis)
  hamiltonian/  operator.py (Hamiltonian, hamiltonian, apply_H, dense_matrix)
                kinetic.py (Kinetic)
  solvers/      eigen.py (dense_eigensolver)
  calculations/ bands.py (band_structure, Bands)
  analytic/     free_electron.py (free_electron_bands)
```

XC, pseudopotentials and IO will get their own subpackages, so that the SCF
loop never imports them by name.

**Data.**

- `Lattice` is a frozen dataclass registered as a pytree. Its only leaf is
  `vectors` (rows, Bohr); `reciprocal` and `volume` are derived. `grad` of a
  function of a `Lattice` returns a `Lattice`, which keeps cell derivatives
  possible later. Input is converted to float64.
- k-points are **fractional** (k = f·B) at every public interface.
- `PlaneWaveBasis` stores only integers and masks: `miller` with shape
  (n_k, N_pad, 3), `mask` with shape (n_k, N_pad), fractional `kpoints`, and
  the static `ecut` and `n_pad`. Cartesian k+G and kinetic energies are
  computed from a `Lattice` when needed, so the path from the cell to the
  energies stays differentiable. The basis is purely combinatorial.
- One batched basis holds all k-points. `basis[i]` returns the same class with
  the k axis removed, which is also what `vmap` hands the mapped function.
- `N_pad` defaults to exactly max_k N_PW and can be overridden with `n_pad=`.
  If it is smaller than that, construction raises `ValueError`. Bucketing
  waits until profiling shows recompilation matters.

**Operators and solver.**

- A Hamiltonian term is a pytree with `prepare(lattice, basis_k)`, which
  returns a prepared pytree with `apply(psi)`. `hamiltonian()` prepares every
  term once per k, so iterative solvers do not repeat the setup on every
  apply. Terms never see padding.
- `apply_H(ham, psi)` acts on blocks `psi` of shape (N_pad, n). It masks the
  input, sums the terms, masks the output, and adds `s·psi` on padded entries.
  Decoupling is therefore enforced centrally, so a new term cannot leak by
  forgetting a mask. The tests require ecut < s ≤ 10·ecut.
- `dense_eigensolver(apply, dim, n_bands)` takes any linear operator and knows
  nothing about plane waves.
- `band_structure(lattice, basis, n_bands, terms=(Kinetic(),), solver=dense_eigensolver)`
  returns `Bands(eigenvalues, eigenvectors, kpoints, basis)`. Eigenvalues have
  shape (n_k, n_bands) in Hartree; eigenvectors have shape
  (n_k, N_pad, n_bands) and are zero on padding. The function raises
  `ValueError` if n_bands > min_k N_PW.

**k-paths.** `special_points_fcc()` returns a dict from label to fractional k,
with ASCII keys (`"G"` for Γ). `kpath(lattice, points, segments, n_points)`
spreads exactly `n_points` points over the segments by Cartesian length. It
returns `KPath(kpoints, distance, tick_positions, tick_labels)`. The tick
labels use Γ, and a break is labelled `"U|K"`; the distance does not advance
across a break.

**Analytic reference.** `jaxdft.analytic.free_electron_bands` exists so that
the validation document can use it without reimplementing physics. The tests
never trust it. They compare it with `tests/support/free_electron.py`, an
independent NumPy enumeration over twice the proven Miller bound, which is
itself checked against the hand-derived degeneracy table.

**Spec gap found while writing the tests.** With a non-diagonal term, physical
eigenvalues can exceed ecut, and the sentinel is only guaranteed to be above
ecut. So the requested bands are guaranteed physical only below ecut. This is
exactly the theory post's rule ("tests compare only eigenvalues below the
cutoff"). The tests follow it everywhere, and the test-only coupling term is
kept weak (a Gershgorin bound of about 0.16 Ha). Requesting all N_PW bands with
a strong potential is legitimate input, but it may return sentinel
eigenvalues.

## 2026-11-05: Milestone 1a implementation

**Pytrees.** `Lattice` and `PlaneWaveBasis` are pytree classes whose
`tree_unflatten` bypasses `__init__`. JAX rebuilds pytrees with tracers,
cotangents and placeholder objects, and validation or dtype conversion in
`__init__` would break on those. Input conversion (to float64, shape checks)
therefore happens only on user construction. `ecut` and `n_pad` are static aux
data of the basis, so changing the cutoff retraces. That is intended, since
the shapes change with it anyway. Prepared terms and `Hamiltonian` use
`register_dataclass`; the sentinel is a static field.

**Basis construction without a k loop.** `PlaneWaveBasis.build` enumerates one
integer box from the proven bound, using the largest |k| in the batch. It
evaluates ½|(f+m)B|² for every k at once, then compacts each row with a stable
`argsort` of the inverted mask. Real entries come first and padding takes
Miller index 0. This runs eagerly on the host, because the output shape depends
on the data. The box is shared across k, which wastes some work when the
k-points differ a lot in |k|. That matters only for construction, not for the
padded arrays the physics sees.

**Operator and solver.**

- `apply_H` is the only place that knows about padding (the sentinel is
  2·ecut).
- `dense_eigensolver` symmetrises the matrix it builds before `eigh`. This
  costs nothing and removes rounding-level anti-Hermitian parts that a future
  term could introduce.
- `band_structure` zeroes eigenvectors on padding explicitly. With LAPACK
  `eigh` on an exactly decoupled block this is already true bit for bit (a
  mutation test confirmed it). The explicit mask makes it a guarantee for
  solvers that don't share that property.
- The whole band structure is one `jit` over a `vmap` over k, with `n_bands`
  and the solver static.

**Mutation testing of the acceptance suite.** The tests had never been run
against an implementation, so a clean first pass proved little. I planted bugs
one at a time and checked that the suite caught them. Each of these was caught:

- terms seeing padded input
- coupled padding rows
- a sentinel far above 10·ecut
- an enumeration bound that ignores |k|
- a 1e-7 error in the kinetic prefactor
- a missing transpose in B
- a 2% cutoff error

Two changes were not caught, both by design:

- `<=` versus `<` in the cutoff test, since tests never put a cutoff on a
  shell.
- A cutoff error of 0.1%. Test cutoffs sit mid-gap, so it selects the same
  plane waves and is physically unobservable.

**Validation document.**

- In the empty lattice, the computed eigenvalues agree bit for bit with the
  library's analytic reference. `eigh` on a diagonal matrix returns the
  diagonal, and both evaluate the same expression. The document says so rather
  than presenting it as a tolerance check.
- The document asserts its own interpretive claims (degeneracies match,
  deviation within tolerance), so a regression breaks the render rather than
  leaving stale prose.

**Plotting and dependencies.** The shared style lives in `jaxdft.plotting.style`.
Inside the package, the docs can import it without `sys.path` manipulation.
It imports altair lazily, and nothing in the physics imports it. It disables
altair's 5000-row cap, because band structures are a few thousand points.
`pandas` joins the `docs` group. I checked the charts visually by rendering
their Vega-Lite specs to PNG with `vl-convert`, in a throwaway environment.
That is not a project dependency.

## 2026-11-05: Test correction, kinetic diagonal tolerance at k+G = 0

Hypothesis found a case where the property test
`test_empty_lattice_physical_block_is_kinetic_diagonal` failed: a cubic cell
with k = (1,1,1) fractional, so one plane wave has k+G = 0 exactly. The two
arithmetic routes, $(\mathbf{f}+\mathbf{m})B$ in the package and
$\mathbf{k} + \mathbf{m}B$ in the test, both round to a kinetic energy of order
1e-32 Ha. The test's purely relative tolerance (`rtol=1e-13`, `atol=0`) cannot
accept rounding at an exact zero. This was a defect in the test, not the code.
I raised it before changing anything, and the agreed fix adds `atol = 1e-14·ecut`,
which follows the theory post's argument that rounding scales with
$\|H_\text{phys}\| \le E_\text{cut}$. The falsifying case is pinned as an
explicit `@example`. I audited the other relative-only comparisons: they either
compare exact zeros with exact zeros or involve no zeros.

## 2026-11-05: Milestone 1b design decisions from theory review

The [1b theory post](../theory/01b_cohen_bergstresser.qmd) was reviewed before
implementation, and the review is kept in `docs/theory/reviews/`. It confirmed
the normalisation. I checked its sharpest claims independently, with a
throwaway NumPy model, before acting on them.

**Matrix-free local potential.** The first draft proposed storing a dense
$\tilde V(\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{G}')$ per k-point. That is $O(N^2)$ per k, multiplied
by $n_k$ under `vmap`, and it is a stored matrix rather than an operator. Each
row has at most 44 non-zeros (shells 3, 8 and 11), independently of the
cutoff. So `prepare` builds a per-k neighbour table and `apply` is a gather and
a sum. The neighbour search runs inside `jit`/`vmap` and so must be jittable:
sorted integer Miller keys plus `searchsorted`, not a host dictionary. Dense
matrices are built only from the operator, as in 1a.

**Off-shell guard in physical units.** The guard must compare $|\mathbf{G}|^2$
in Bohr⁻² against the shells at $a_\text{CB}$. Dimensionless shell indices are
invariant under isotropic scaling, so a guard on them would accept any lattice
constant. The review pointed this out; my draft had the reason subtly wrong.

**Kept: physical-unit shell matching, not integer cubic indices.** The review
proposed exact integer keys. They are exact for fcc only, and the separation
between shells makes a $10^{-8}$ relative window unambiguous anyway.

**Tests sharpened.**

- The indirect gap is tested as the minimum along Δ, with an interiority
  check. The level at X lies within the tolerance of the paper's value, so a
  test of the level at X would pass on the wrong quantity.
- Inversion parity gives the first eigenvector test, as a trace over the
  level's projector.
- Pairing is tested along the X–W line, with a negative control at a generic
  face point.
- The test cutoff is 6 Ha, where all Table I splittings have converged to
  about 1 meV.
- Physics tolerances are 0.15 or 0.25 eV per entry, derived from the paper's
  stated rounding and convergence. Numerical tolerances are 1e-10 Ha for
  eigenvalue comparisons and 1e-8 Ha for grouping degenerate levels.

**Not adopted.** A test of the minimum's position (0.855 X ± 0.01) would be a
regression value: the only sources are our own model and a secondary
reproduction of the same model. It is reported in the validation document
instead. DFTK is deferred to the SCF milestone.

## 2026-11-05: Milestone 1b public API, agreed before implementation

Settled in four question rounds with the project lead before any 1b test or
code was written. The changes to the 1a API were approved as part of these
rounds.

**The system object is `Structure`, not `Lattice`.** `Structure` is a pytree:
a `Lattice`, fractional `positions` with shape (n_atoms, 3) as a leaf, per-atom
`weights` with shape (n_atoms,) as a leaf defaulting to 1, and static `species`
labels. It represents any periodic configuration: a bulk crystal, a slab, or a
molecule in a vacuum box. "Crystal" was rejected because it reads oddly for the
last two. Positions are always stored fractional. The decisions that follow:

- `Structure.from_cartesian(cell, positions, species, unit=...)` takes the cell
  and positions in the same unit, `"Angstrom"` or `"Bohr"`. There is no default,
  so every call states its unit. It converts once.
- Weights are not range-checked. Their physical range is [0, 1], but
  finite-difference checks at λ = 1 need to step past it.
- Atoms are mapped to pseudopotentials by species label, through a dict held by
  the term.
- Factories live in a subpackage, one module each:
  `structure/builders/{fcc,diamond,empty}.py`. `Lattice.fcc` moves there as
  `fcc_lattice`, so `Lattice` keeps only its general constructor. Code used by
  several builders goes in a shared module when it appears.
- The term protocol becomes `prepare(structure, basis_k)`, and
  `band_structure(structure, basis, ...)` and `hamiltonian(structure, ...)`
  follow. The 1a tests are updated mechanically. The empty lattice is
  `empty(lattice)`. `PlaneWaveBasis.build`, `kpath` and `free_electron_bands`
  keep taking a `Lattice`, because they involve no atoms.

**Pseudopotential protocol** (and the matching update to `CLAUDE.md`). The
literal `(G) -> (V_loc, V_nl)` signature was dropped after a discussion. The
two parts are different kinds of object: a local form factor v̂(q), against
nonlocal projectors depending on k+G and k+G′ separately. A tuple would force
us to guess the nonlocal interface before anything exists to test it. The
protocol is now:

- `local(q) -> v̂(q)`: the atomic Fourier transform, in Ha·Bohr³,
  cell-independent. The `LocalPotential` term applies
  Ṽ(G) = Ω⁻¹ Σⱼ λⱼ e^{−iG·τⱼ} v̂ⱼ(|G|).
- `local_support: float | None`: the q beyond which v̂ is exactly zero.
  `None` means unbounded. The gather-based term refuses an unbounded
  pseudopotential, pointing to the FFT term that comes with SCF.
- An optional host-side `validate(...)` hook. `band_structure` calls
  `term.validate(structure)` before tracing, and `LocalPotential` forwards it
  to each pseudopotential. Cohen–Bergstresser raises if a non-zero |G|² within
  its support is off its tabulated shells, comparing in physical units.
- Nonlocal methods are added, additively, in the milestone that first needs
  them, with their own Hamiltonian term.

**Cohen–Bergstresser.** `jaxdft.pseudo.cohen_bergstresser.silicon()` returns
a `CohenBergstresser` holding a_CB and the form factors in publication units
(Å, Ry), converted at construction. Only Si is included, so no untested data
ships.

**Units.** `jaxdft/units.py` holds CODATA 2022 constants and a `convert`
helper. Units are cross-cutting (structure, pseudo, plotting), so no
subpackage owns them.

**Analysis.** A `jaxdft/analysis/` subpackage holds the tools both tests and
docs need: degenerate-level grouping, inversion parity, the VBM energy
reference, and the minimum of a band along a segment. The minimum is found by
dense vmapped sampling followed by bracketed golden-section refinement on the
host. An autodiff-based search (via group velocities) was deferred to a
dedicated milestone: the k-dependent basis makes dE/dk well defined only
within a fixed basis.

**Reference data.** `reference/cohen_bergstresser_1966/si_table1.json` holds
Table I's Si row, in eV as printed, with experiment and calculation separate,
a tolerance class per entry, and source metadata. A README says it was
transcribed by hand from the scan.
